title: Electricity 2026
key_claim: The IEA's annual Electricity 2026 report has a special focus on grids and flexibility and, for the first time, updates its supply-side flexibility analysis with 'further examination of falling capture rates for solar and wind generation and the spectacular growth of battery storage systems'; utility-scale battery additions reached a record 63 GW in 2024 (total 124 GW) with project costs down ~40% to ~USD 150/kWh, while only ~100 GW of demand response is utilised globally; markets with high shares of solar and wind face periods of overabundance requiring measures from output control to storage to 'offering free electricity to customers'.
frame_summary: The IEA frames falling capture rates and periods of renewable overabundance as the defining new challenge of the 'Age of Electricity', arguing that securely integrating cheap variable renewables now hinges on a large expansion of system flexibility rather than on generation cost.
notes: Structural anchor: IEA flagship annual report, canonical source naming the falling-capture-rate framing. Body paraphrases (no verbatim quote). Published 06 February 2026 (3-6m band). Flexibility chapter at https://www.iea.org/reports/electricity-2026/flexibility.

title: Quarterly Energy Dynamics Q1 2026
key_claim: In Q1 2026 the National Electricity Market saw negative or zero prices in 14.9% of dispatch intervals, down 3.0 percentage points from 18.0% in Q1 2025, with all regions except Victoria (26.2%) recording year-on-year reductions and South Australia highest at 31.3%; combined battery charge and discharge accounted for 32% of price-setting dispatch intervals, making batteries the most frequent price-setting technology; the average spot price during negative-price intervals rose from -$35.4/MWh to -$17.7/MWh and the NEM-wide negative-price impact fell from $6.4/MWh to $2.6/MWh, even as solar and wind network curtailment nearly doubled to an average 296 MW.
frame_summary: AEMO frames Australia's rapid battery build-out as materially reshaping the market, showing that large and small batteries have absorbed midday surpluses and pushed the frequency and depth of negative prices down year-on-year even as renewable penetration rose.
notes: Tier 1 market-operator data. Used for geographic breadth (Australia) and as the strongest counter-evidence: batteries reducing negative-price incidence. No verbatim_quote recorded (large PDF); key_claim is a faithful summary cross-checked against AEMO media release 'Renewables lift supply share as batteries re-shape energy markets', 30/04/2026.

publisher: Aurora Energy Research (reported via PV Tech)
title: European Co-location Markets Attractiveness Report (Germany, Great Britain and Bulgaria top Europe's co-location investment rankings for 2026)
key_claim: Aurora Energy Research's European Co-location Markets Attractiveness Report finds negative-pricing hours increased sharply in 2025, with Spain, the Netherlands and Germany each recording more than 500 hours; it forecasts deeper capture-price cannibalisation by 2030, with solar discounts approaching 50% in Iberia and onshore-wind discounts exceeding 25% in Germany, and curtailment across key European markets rising from more than 10 TWh in 2024 to approximately 33 TWh by 2030; co-located capacity reached 6.3 GW in 2025 (solar-plus-storage >60% of deployments) with more than 1,600 GW of renewable and storage projects awaiting grid connection, and two-sided CfDs supporting co-location in I-SEM, Great Britain, France, Romania and Estonia.
frame_summary: Aurora argues that deteriorating wholesale conditions - negative prices and capture-price cannibalisation - are now the primary driver pushing developers toward co-located storage and two-sided CfDs, making flexibility rather than pure generation the basis of a bankable renewables investment case.
notes: Tier 2 institutional research (Aurora) reported via PV Tech (publisher). Provides the forward forecast quant (2030 cannibalisation, curtailment trajectory) and the co-location adaptation.

title: Europe's negative electricity price hours double in Q1 amid renewables surpluses, market imbalances
key_claim: Analysis by consultancy Ricardo (WSP Group) of ENTSO-E data finds EU-27 day-ahead markets cleared 1,223 hours below zero in Q1 2026, more than double the 593 hours in Q1 2025 and over ten times the 119 hours of Q1 2022; Spain alone accounted for 347 hours (16% of Q1 trading hours) having never recorded a Q1 negative hour before 2023; in April 2026 Germany cleared 123 of 720 hours below zero (deepest -413.8 EUR/MWh) and 4,559 GWh, or 46.7%, of the month's solar output was delivered during negative-price hours.
frame_summary: The piece argues that negative prices are becoming a structural, not episodic, feature of European day-ahead markets and that the hours of deepest oversupply are precisely the hours when solar and wind monetise below zero, exposing merchant renewable revenue.
notes: Tier 3 trade press carrying a named consultancy (Ricardo/WSP) analysis of ENTSO-E Transparency Platform data. On-page Spain figure is 347 hours (search snippet's 397 was wrong; used verified on-page value).

title: Solar capture factors fall across Europe as negative price hours surge in key markets
key_claim: Reporting Pexapark analysis, pv magazine finds solar capture factors fell sharply year-on-year in April 2026: France to around 0.10 from 0.42 (a 75% decline), Germany to about 0.26 from 0.40 (about a third), Poland to about 0.40 from 0.54, and Italy to about 0.71 from 0.75 (its second-lowest on record); Spain's capture factor dropped to about 0.18 in February 2026 from 0.71 a year earlier, with 148 negative-price hours that month versus zero the year before, indicating oversupply is now emerging even in winter.
frame_summary: The article argues that capture-factor collapse across five European markets is driven by structural solar oversupply rather than fuel or geopolitical price swings, and that European solar may be entering a new phase where severe midday oversupply is a recurring structural condition.
notes: Tier 3 trade press reporting Pexapark's capture-factor analysis. Used for the capture-factor quantification anchors; distinct author (Patrick Jowett) from the 08/05 Ricardo piece.

title: Dispatch from Germany | May '26
key_claim: The German government approved a draft law introducing auctions for new government-supported gas-fired power plants and other capacity to back up wind and solar and guarantee security of supply as coal is phased out, with first tenders planned for later in 2026; the move drew criticism, and states' energy ministers opposed proposed rooftop-solar cuts, arguing they could deter investment.
frame_summary: Clean Energy Wire reports that Germany is turning to procured dispatchable gas backup and support-scheme changes as it grapples with integrating a rapidly growing wind and solar fleet, illustrating how the flexibility and firming problem is now shaping national policy.
notes: Tier 3 specialist journalism. Used for the firming/backup market-design response (German gas-backup capacity auctions) and the political tension over solar support.

title: European Solar Capture Factors Collapse as April Oversupply Triggers Wave of Negative Prices
key_claim: Pexapark reports that in April 2026 the longest continuous negative-price period in Germany reached 17 hours (up from 7 hours in April 2025), that France's energy regulator CRE has proposed replacing the solar-capture reference price in large-scale CfDs with a baseload index and reducing compensation during negative-price periods while explicitly favouring co-located PV and batteries, and concludes that 'solar deployment is now advancing faster than system flexibility', with current BESS penetration still too limited to materially compress day-ahead spreads or absorb large-scale midday surpluses at the system level.
frame_summary: Pexapark, a renewables-market advisory, argues that midday oversupply has shifted from isolated events to recurring structural conditions and that the policy and investment response - CfD redesign and co-located storage - is running behind the pace of solar deployment.
